title: What's the deal with diplomatic immunity?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain diplomatic immunity, starting with its roots in ancient practice (Hammurabi's violation, Genghis Khan's envoy and the Khwarazmian ruler, Darius I and the Spartan envoys) and its codification in England after the Russian envoy debt incident under Elizabeth I and Peter the Great. They cover the core principles of personal inviolability, extraterritoriality, and functional necessity, the 1961 UN Vienna Convention, and how immunity covers families, domestic workers, and international organizations. Abuses are discussed, including unpaid New York parking tickets (about $16.7 million by July 2011, Russia the largest debtor), a Mexican attache stealing BlackBerrys at the White House, a 1979 Burmese ambassador's killing of his wife, human trafficking by diplomatic employers, and a 2013 Nairobi crash by a U.S. embassy officer. They also discuss persona non grata declarations, the 2011 Raymond Davis case in Pakistan, and the 2010 Haiti cholera outbreak involving UN peacekeepers. The episode closes with listener mail about an ejection seat misfire survivor (Lt. Keith Gallagher) and a request for listener stories.
topics: Peter the Great debt incident England

segments.title: Opening banter and topic setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about band leaders and a Lethal Weapon 2 reference, then Chuck explains the topic came from listener suggestions on Twitter.

segments.title: Ancient origins: Hammurabi and Genghis Khan
segments.summary: The hosts say diplomatic protection is at least 4,000 years old, citing Hammurabi as the first documented violator. They discuss Genghis Khan's envoy to the Khwarazmian ruler, which was violated and led to the Mongols' retaliation.

segments.title: Darius I and the Spartan envoys; Rome and the Holy Roman Empire
segments.summary: Darius I refused to retaliate when Spartans killed his envoys, saying it would violate human law. The hosts say that after Rome fell, the protection of diplomats remained strongly established. They describe the purpose of diplomats as messengers and brokers of peace.

segments.title: Safe passage and diplomats today
segments.summary: Diplomats need safe passage home if talks fail, as with Nazi Germany giving passage to Allied diplomats in World War Two. The hosts discuss the Benghazi attack and the difference between ambassadors and diplomats, and note that immunity extends to families and domestic staff.

segments.title: Personal inviolability and extraterritoriality
segments.summary: The hosts define personal inviolability as the protection of a diplomat's person and extraterritoriality as the treatment of diplomatic premises and cars as the sending country's soil. They explain that police can detain a diplomat, but courts must dismiss charges.

segments.title: Peter the Great, Elizabeth I, and the debt incident
segments.summary: A Russian diplomat was held over unpaid debts at an English pub. Peter the Great asked Elizabeth I for his release, and England later passed an act making foreign embassies inviolable and outside jurisdiction, including debt.

segments.title: Corruption, prosecution and parking tickets
segments.summary: The hosts discuss corruption and prosecution of diplomats. In July 2011, unpaid New York City tickets totaled $16.7 million, with Russia owing the most. The hosts joke about double-parking.

segments.title: Human trafficking of domestic workers
segments.summary: The hosts describe how domestic workers of diplomats can be trafficked because a diplomat's home is treated as sovereign soil outside US labor law. They say this violates both American and international law.

segments.title: Persona non grata, Raymond Davis, and the Haiti cholera outbreak
segments.summary: The hosts explain persona non grata, and the 2011 Raymond Davis case in Pakistan, in which the US agreed to recall a list of Americans. They also cover the UN's invoking of immunity after cholera killed Haitians in 2010, and the functional necessity principle.

segments.title: Diplomatic abuse stories
segments.summary: The hosts recount a Mexican attache who took BlackBerrys at the White House, a 1979 Burmese ambassador who killed and burned his wife in Sri Lanka, and a July 2013 Nairobi crash involving a US embassy officer.

segments.title: Listener mail: ejection seat misfire and call for tips
segments.summary: A listener named Matt writes about Lt. Keith Gallagher, a Navy navigator whose ejection seat misfired. The hosts ask listeners to send in stories and suggestions.
